topic.title: A one-time 5% tax on billionaires: why can't they just pay it in cash?

title: Why can't billionaires just pay a 5% tax? 🤔
description:
Why can't a billionaire just write the cheque for a one-time 5% tax?
An illustrative $100 billion fortune, a 5% bill paid over five years and an assumed cash share, computed: the money is in shares, not in the bank. No real person's wealth, no side taken on any vote. Speak to a licensed financial adviser in your country before making financial decisions.
Illustrative only. Not financial advice.

lines.text: Why can't a billionaire just pay a tax bill of $5.00B?
California votes on a one-time 5% billionaire tax, paid over 5 years. On an illustrative $100,000,000,000 fortune, that's $1.00B a year.
Easy. He's super rich. Just pay it!
Worth it, yes. In cash? No. Say just 0.5% is cash. That's $500.0M.
The other $99.50B is shares. You can't pay tax with shares.
So even in year one, he's short $500.0M?
Exactly. So he sells shares, or borrows against them. Selling that much can push the price down.
Rich on paper. Short on cash. That's the real answer to...

Beats vote/where/short/sell: the shortfall ($5.00B bill vs $2.00B cash = short $3.00B, so he must sell or borrow) assumes the whole bill is due at once, but the measure the video names (Prop 40, California, 3 Nov 2026) can be paid in five annual installments (NBC Los Angeles; CA Budget Center; ITEP) - $1B a year, less than the assumed $2B cash - and lets illiquid assets be deferred until sold (Northern Trust, ITEP). Hides a decisive term; the conclusion is not supported. Fix: either drop 'California votes' and make it a hypothetical one-time tax due in full now, or tell the installment option and redo the cash gap.

Verify item checked: Prop 40 is a one-time 5% tax on net worth above $1B for residents as of Jan 1, 2026, on the Nov 3, 2026 ballot (Wikipedia; AP via ABC7; NBC LA), payable over five annual installments (NBC LA) - confirmed and current. Neutral on the vote, no real person's wealth named: OK.
Minor (not a reason alone): plan description ends with the disclaimer but lacks the profile's 'speak to a licensed financial adviser in your country' line.
